## Comparing penguin body mass
I use Python to calculate average body mass for each penguin species, then pass the summary to R to visualize the comparison.
Data: Palmer Penguins, provided through the Python palmerpenguins package.
Then add a Python chunk to load the data:
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
penguins.head()

  species     island  bill_length_mm  ...  body_mass_g     sex  year
0  Adelie  Torgersen            39.1  ...       3750.0    male  2007
1  Adelie  Torgersen            39.5  ...       3800.0  female  2007
2  Adelie  Torgersen            40.3  ...       3250.0  female  2007
3  Adelie  Torgersen             NaN  ...          NaN     NaN  2007
4  Adelie  Torgersen            36.7  ...       3450.0  female  2007

[5 rows x 8 columns]
penguins stores the dataset. .head() displays the first five rows so you can inspect its columns.
Next, add a second Python chunk:
penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["species", "body_mass_g"])

mass_summary = (
    penguins_clean.groupby("species", as_index=False)
    .agg(mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"))
)

mass_summary

     species  mean_mass_g
0     Adelie  3700.662252
1  Chinstrap  3733.088235
2     Gentoo  5076.016260
Here’s what it does:

title: Penguin body mass with Python and R
text:
Visualizing the summary in R
I pass the summary calculated in Python to R using reticulate.

mass_summary_r <- py$mass_summary
mass_summary_r

    species mean_mass_g
1    Adelie    3700.662
2 Chinstrap    3733.088
3    Gentoo    5076.016


This is the key bonus step:

py$mass_summary accesses the object you created in Python.
Reticulate converts the Python pandas DataFrame into an R data frame.
<- assigns it to the R object mass_summary_r.

Now add a plot using that transferred data:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mass_summary_r, aes(x = species, y = mean_mass_g)) +
geom_col() +
labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Mean body mass (g)"
) +
theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Mean penguin body mass by species, calculated in Python and plotted in R.





geom_col() draws bars using your already-calculated means. R is using Python’s result here, which demonstrates the required object transfer.
Gentoo penguins had the highest average body mass in this dataset, at approximately 5,076 g. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins had similar averages, at about 3,701 g and 3,733 g, respectively. These means summarize differences between species but do not show variation among individual penguins or how much their body masses overlap.

title: How does penguin body mass differ by species?
text:
Compare average body mass
I exclude penguins with missing species or body mass before calculating the number of observations and average body mass for each species.

penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["species", "body_mass_g"])

summary = (
    penguins_clean.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(count="count", mean_mass_g="mean")
    .round(1)
)

summary








count
mean_mass_g


species






Adelie
151
3700.7


Chinstrap
68
3733.1


Gentoo
123
5076.0







Here’s what the code does:

dropna(…) removes rows missing values needed for this analysis.
groupby(“species”) separates the observations by species.
.agg(…) calculates each species’ count and mean body mass.
.round(1) rounds the results to one decimal place.
summary displays the resulting table.

## Visualize the comparison
The chart below compares average body mass across species.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar(summary.index, summary["mean_mass_g"])
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Average body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Average penguin body mass by species")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Average body mass by penguin species, excluding missing measurements.

title: How does penguin body mass differ by species?
text:
Findings
Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass in this dataset. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have more similar average body masses.
These averages describe the sampled penguins. The chart does not show variation within each species or account for differences in sex or island.
The plotting code uses the summary table you already calculated:

ax.bar(…) draws one bar per species.
Axis labels identify the categories and measurement units.
fig-cap adds a caption.
The fig- label identifies this output as a figure.
echo: true explicitly keeps the code visible.

The data were collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Antarctica LTER and are available under the CC0 licence.

title: Do penguins with longer flippers weigh more?
text:
Prepare the measurements
I remove rows missing either measurement so that each plotted penguin has both a flipper length and a body mass.

keep <- complete.cases(penguins[c("flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g")])
penguins_clean <- penguins[keep, ]

data.frame(
    original_rows = nrow(penguins),
    retained_rows = nrow(penguins_clean),
    removed_rows = sum(!keep)
)

  original_rows retained_rows removed_rows
1           344           342            2

title: Do penguins with longer flippers weigh more?
text:
Plot the relationship

ggplot(
    penguins_clean,
    aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Penguin body mass versus flipper length, coloured by species.

title: Do penguins with longer flippers weigh more?
text:
Findings
Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass in this sample. Gentoo penguins tend to have longer flippers and greater body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.
The overall pattern partly reflects differences between species. This plot shows an association; it does not establish that longer flippers cause greater body mass.
